title: HE ACCUSED HIS FATHER’S GENERAL OF SLEEPING WITH HIS CONCUBINE—AND WITH ONE QUESTION, HE BEGAN LOSING HIS KINGDOM
paragraphs: HE ACCUSED HIS FATHER’S GENERAL OF SLEEPING WITH HIS CONCUBINE—AND WITH ONE QUESTION, HE BEGAN LOSING HIS KINGDOM

One accusation. One furious commander. One collapsing throne. But behind the scandal of Ish-bosheth and Abner was a terrifying truth: you can wear a crown, hold a position, and fight desperately to protect something God has already appointed someone else to receive.
“And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” — 2 Samuel 3:7, KJV
Imagine being a king.
You sit on your father's throne. People bow when you enter. Soldiers guard your doors. Your name is spoken with the respect reserved for royalty.
But there is something you know when the palace grows quiet.
The man commanding your army is more powerful than you.
And the kingdom you inherited is slowly slipping away.
Then one day, you confront that man with an accusation so personal, so politically explosive, that it threatens to destroy the fragile arrangement keeping you in power.
You accuse him of sleeping with your dead father's concubine.
And instead of defending himself calmly, he explodes.
Not merely with anger.
With a declaration that will change the direction of the kingdom.
He will take his strength, his influence, and his loyalty elsewhere.
He will help deliver the kingdom to David.
And you?
You will be left sitting on a throne you cannot defend.
This is not a fictional palace drama.
This happened in the biblical account of Ish-bosheth and Abner.
And what makes this story so unsettling is that the accusation was only the visible spark.
The deeper fire had been burning for years.
Because sometimes the greatest danger is not the enemy standing outside your gates.
Sometimes it is the unstable foundation beneath the throne you are desperately trying to protect.
And before we are finished, there is a question this ancient scandal will place before every one of us.
What happens when the thing you are fighting hardest to keep is the very thing God is calling you to surrender?
The story begins after the death of King Saul.
Israel is fractured. Saul and his son Jonathan have fallen in battle. David, whom God had previously chosen and Samuel had anointed, has become king over Judah.
But the rest of Israel has not yet united under David.
Abner, the commander of Saul's army, takes Ish-bosheth, another son of Saul, and establishes him as king over Israel.
Scripture says:

“But Abner the son of Ner, captain of Saul's host, took Ishbosheth the son of Saul, and brought him over to Mahanaim; And made him king over Gilead, and over the Ashurites, and over Jezreel, and over Ephraim, and over Benjamin, and over all Israel.” — 2 Samuel 2:8–9, KJV
Notice something important.
The text does not present Ish-bosheth as a man who rose to power through his own military strength.
Abner took him.
Abner brought him.
Abner made him king.
The distinction matters.
Ish-bosheth possessed royal blood, but Abner possessed the military influence that helped sustain his reign.
And while Ish-bosheth occupied his father's throne, David's house continued growing stronger.
The Bible summarizes the conflict with devastating simplicity:
“Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.” — 2 Samuel 3:1, KJV
Stronger and stronger.
Weaker and weaker.
Two houses moving in opposite directions.
One advancing toward the fulfillment of God's declared purpose.
The other struggling through the decline of Saul's dynasty.
And right in the middle stood a man named Abner.
A commander whose influence was increasing even while the house he served was weakening.
Second Samuel 3:6 says that Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.
Then came Rizpah.
Her name appears almost suddenly.
No dramatic introduction.
No recorded speech.
No explanation of her feelings.
Just one sentence identifying her as Saul's concubine and the daughter of Aiah.
And then the accusation.
Ish-bosheth confronts Abner:
“Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” — 2 Samuel 3:7, KJV
The ancient Hebrew makes the accusation direct.
מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָה אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי
Maddua bata el-pilegesh avi?
“Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?”
The expression “gone in to” is a Hebrew way of referring to sexual relations in this context.
This was not a complaint about an inappropriate conversation.
Ish-bosheth was accusing Abner of sexual involvement with Rizpah.
But here is where careful reading becomes essential.
Scripture records the accusation. It does not independently establish that Abner actually slept with Rizpah.
That distinction matters.
The Bible does not give us permission to turn an allegation into a proven fact.
And Rizpah herself is never given a voice in this confrontation.
We do not know what she said, what she wanted, or whether the accusation was true.
What we do know is that the allegation carried enormous political weight.
In the ancient royal world, relationships involving a former king's wives or concubines could have implications for claims to royal authority.

Later in Israel's history, Absalom publicly took his father's concubines during his rebellion against David (2 Samuel 16:21–22). In another royal succession dispute, Solomon interpreted Adonijah's request concerning Abishag as politically threatening (1 Kings 2:13–25).
Those passages help us understand why Ish-bosheth's accusation could be more than a private moral complaint.
It could suggest that Abner was reaching for privileges associated with kingship.
The man who helped place Ish-bosheth on the throne might now be suspected of reaching toward that throne himself.
Imagine the fear behind that possibility.
You are already losing a war.
Your military commander is growing more powerful.
Your father's dynasty is weakening.
And now you suspect that the man keeping your kingdom standing may be crossing a boundary that threatens your own royal authority.
So you confront him.
But what happens next is not what Ish-bosheth appears to have expected.
Abner erupts.
“Then was Abner very wroth for the words of Ishbosheth...” — 2 Samuel 3:8, KJV
The Hebrew describes Abner as becoming exceedingly angry.
And his response reveals something about the relationship between these two men.
He reminds Ish-bosheth of everything he has done for Saul's family.
He has shown loyalty to Saul's house.
He has not handed Ish-bosheth over to David.
He has protected the dynasty.
And now, after all that service, he is being challenged over a woman.
His words begin with a fierce expression:
“Am I a dog's head, which against Judah do shew kindness this day unto the house of Saul thy father...?” — 2 Samuel 3:8, KJV
Abner feels insulted.
Humiliated.
Accused by the very king whose position he has helped preserve.
And then comes the turning point.
Abner swears that he will do for David what the Lord has promised.
“To translate the kingdom from the house of Saul, and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba.” — 2 Samuel 3:10, KJV
Read that carefully.
Abner does not merely threaten to resign.
He announces his intention to transfer the kingdom from Saul's house to David.
But the most revealing part is that Abner acknowledges the Lord's promise concerning David.
That raises a deeply uncomfortable question.
If Abner knew that God had promised the kingdom to David, why had he continued strengthening Saul's house against him?
The text does not disclose every motive in Abner's heart.
We should not pretend it does.
But it clearly shows that Abner understood the divine promise by the time he made this declaration.
And now, after a personal insult, he is suddenly ready to help bring that promise to fulfillment.
That is a warning worth carrying into our own lives.
A person can speak accurately about God's will while still being driven by wounded pride.
Not every correct religious statement comes from a surrendered heart.
Not every sudden change of direction is evidence of repentance.
Sometimes people move toward the right destination for reasons that still need to be examined.
Abner's decision aligned with the promised future of David's kingship.
But the immediate trigger was his anger at Ish-bosheth.
The Bible allows us to see both realities without pretending we know everything about his motives.
And then comes one of the most painful verses in the entire account.
“And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him.” — 2 Samuel 3:11, KJV
He could not answer.
Not another word.
The king who had confronted his commander was now silent before him.
Why?
Because he was afraid.
The Hebrew closes the verse with:
כִּי יָרֵא אֹתוֹ
Ki yare oto.
“Because he feared him.”
Think about that.
Ish-bosheth wore the crown.
Abner held the power.
Ish-bosheth possessed the title.
Abner commanded the fear.
And when the commander threatened to abandon him, the king could not even answer.
There are people reading this who understand that kind of silence.
Perhaps you have a position that looks secure to everyone else, but privately you know how dependent you are on someone else's approval.
Perhaps you have built your identity around a relationship, a reputation, a ministry role, a business, or a title.
You appear confident until the person holding everything together threatens to walk away.
Suddenly, your voice disappears.
You cannot speak.
You cannot confront.
You cannot imagine life without the thing you have been leaning on.
And the frightening question is not simply whether you might lose it.
It is whether you have allowed it to become the foundation of your identity.
There is a difference between receiving help from people and making people your ultimate security.
There is a difference between appreciating influence and worshiping influence.
There is a difference between faithfully stewarding a responsibility and desperately clinging to a position God never promised would last forever.
Ish-bosheth's fear exposes the vulnerability of his kingship.
And it invites us to examine the foundations beneath our own lives.
But there is another detail in this story that should disturb us.
Rizpah.
A woman whose name becomes the center of a confrontation between powerful men.
A woman whose alleged sexual involvement carries political consequences.
A woman whose perspective the narrative does not record.
It would be easy to treat her as nothing more than the scandal that brought down a king's confidence.
But Scripture does not leave Rizpah's story there.
Later, in 2 Samuel 21, she appears again.
And this time, we see her grief.
After two of her sons are executed in connection with a judgment involving Saul's house, Rizpah spreads sackcloth upon a rock and guards their bodies from birds and wild animals.
Day after day.
Through exposure and sorrow.
A grieving mother refusing to abandon her dead.
When David hears what she has done, he takes action to gather and bury the remains of Saul, Jonathan, and those who had been executed.
The woman who was once mentioned in a royal accusation becomes a figure of extraordinary maternal devotion.
Her story reminds us that people are more than the scandals in which their names appear.
More than rumors.
More than the way powerful people discuss them.
More than the worst chapter attached to their lives.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that reminder more than anything else.
You have been called names.
You have been misunderstood.
Your story has been told by people who never asked what really happened.
Maybe your name has traveled through conversations you were never invited into.
Maybe people remember the accusation but not the tears.
The controversy but not the suffering.
The label but not the human being carrying it.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ does not need gossip to tell Him who you are.
He knows the truth.
He sees what others cannot see.
And His knowledge of you is deeper than both the accusations against you and the excuses you make for yourself.
He knows your wounds.
He also knows your sins.
He is neither deceived by your reputation nor limited by your past.
That is why the Gospel is not simply a message that says you are better than people think.
It is the far greater announcement that sinners can be forgiven and made new through Jesus Christ.
Not because our lives contain no guilt.
But because His mercy is greater than the guilt of those who repent and trust in Him.
And now the story takes another turn.
After Abner's furious declaration, he sends messengers to David, offering to help bring Israel under David's rule.
The accusation has become a political rupture.
The rupture has become a transfer of allegiance.
And the commander who once sustained Ish-bosheth's kingdom is now negotiating with the man destined to replace him.
Yet even here, the Bible refuses to give us a simple story of heroes and villains.
Abner will later be murdered by Joab.
David will publicly mourn Abner and condemn the killing.
Ish-bosheth will eventually be murdered by two of his own captains.
And David will condemn their crime as well, ordering judgment against the killers (2 Samuel 4:9–12).
David does not celebrate the murder of Ish-bosheth as a convenient way to secure the throne.
That matters.
God's promise did not make treachery righteous.
Divine sovereignty did not excuse human wickedness.
And the coming of David's kingdom did not mean every act committed along the way had God's approval.
There is a lesson here for anyone who has ever justified a sinful method because the goal seemed spiritual.
A good destination does not sanctify every road taken to reach it.
You cannot make betrayal holy simply by attaching God's name to it.
You cannot turn cruelty into righteousness by calling it destiny.
And you cannot assume that because God brings good out of a terrible situation, the terrible actions themselves were good.
The Lord is sovereign.
Human beings remain morally accountable.
Both truths stand together.
And that brings us to the deeper story running beneath this entire chapter.
David had been anointed before he possessed the full kingdom.
There was a long and painful distance between God's promise and its public fulfillment.
He endured danger, displacement, opposition, and waiting.
He had opportunities to seize power through violence against Saul, yet he refused to kill the Lord's anointed king (1 Samuel 24; 26).
David was not a sinless man. The Scriptures later expose his grievous failures.
But in those earlier encounters with Saul, he demonstrated a willingness to wait rather than secure the throne through murder.
And in this account, the kingdom begins moving toward him through a conflict he did not initiate.
There is something deeply searching about that.
How much damage do we do because we cannot bear to wait?
How many relationships have we wounded because we were desperate to be recognized?
How many compromises have we justified because we thought God's promise needed our manipulation?
How many times have we confused control with faithfulness?
Sometimes we are terrified that if we stop forcing the outcome, everything will fall apart.
But faith does not mean refusing to act responsibly.
It means refusing to make disobedience our strategy for obtaining what we desire.
It means trusting God enough to obey Him even when obedience seems slower than manipulation.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question in this story is not whether you resemble Ish-bosheth or Abner.
Perhaps it is whether you recognize something of both men in yourself.
Like Ish-bosheth, you may be afraid of losing control.
Like Abner, you may be furious because someone questioned your loyalty or wounded your pride.
You may know what Scripture says and still struggle to submit your motives to it.
You may defend your position while neglecting your character.
You may demand respect while withholding humility.
You may want God's blessing without wanting God's correction.
And if that is where this story finds you, do not run from the conviction.
Bring it into the light.
Because the Bible was never given merely to entertain us with the failures of ancient kings.
It also exposes the human heart.
The same heart that can hide pride behind service.
Fear behind authority.
Ambition behind loyalty.
And insecurity behind anger.
But the story of Scripture does not end with Ish-bosheth.
Or Abner.
Or even David.
It moves toward a greater King.
Jesus Christ.
David's kingdom was an important part of God's unfolding redemptive plan, but David himself was not the final answer to humanity's deepest problem.
Israel needed more than political unity.
And we need more than improved circumstances.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness for real sins.
We need a righteousness we cannot manufacture.
We need a Savior who can rescue us from the guilt and power of sin.
And that is why Jesus is not simply another character in the long history of kings.
He is the promised Son of David whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32–33).
Where earthly rulers are weakened by fear, pride, and death, Christ reigns with perfect righteousness.
Where human kingdoms are shaken by betrayal, His kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28).
Where sinners attempt to protect themselves through power, Jesus willingly humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:5–8).
Consider the contrast.
Ish-bosheth feared losing his throne.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
Abner reacted to an accusation with fierce anger and a change of allegiance.
Jesus, when falsely accused and oppressed, entrusted Himself to the Father who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).
Human rulers struggled over a kingdom.
Christ came to save people who had rebelled against the King of heaven.
And at Calvary, the innocent Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
This is the center of the Gospel.
Not that every scandal will disappear.
Not that every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we wish.
Not that following Jesus guarantees an earthly throne.
But that through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and eternal life are offered to those who repent and believe.
The apostle Paul writes:
Peace with God.
Not merely peace with your circumstances.
Not merely relief from public embarrassment.
Not merely vindication before people who doubted you.
Peace with the holy God against whom we have sinned.
That is the grace we desperately need.
And that grace does not encourage us to hide our sin.
It calls us to confess it.
To turn from it.
To stop pretending that appearances can make us righteous.
To stop treating religious language as a substitute for surrender.
Because there is no crown worth keeping if keeping it requires you to lose your integrity.
No reputation worth protecting through deceit.
No position worth preserving through cruelty.
No earthly kingdom worth choosing over the kingdom of Christ.
Maybe your throne is not made of gold.
Maybe it is your pride.
Your need to be right.
Your obsession with being respected.
Your refusal to apologize.
Your fear of being forgotten.
Your secret dependence on people's praise.
Maybe you have been holding something so tightly that you no longer remember what trusting God feels like.
And the question is no longer whether you can keep control.
The question is whether you will surrender control to the Lord who is worthy of your trust.
Not every loss is God's judgment.
Not every closed door is divine rejection.
Not every betrayal means you have stepped outside His will.
We must never use Ish-bosheth's story as a formula for interpreting every painful event in our own lives.
But the account does teach us that human power is fragile, God's declared purposes are not defeated by human opposition, and pride can turn an already unstable situation into disaster.
And above all, the wider biblical story teaches us to place our hope in the King who cannot fail.
Maybe you have made mistakes that still embarrass you.
Maybe you have reacted in anger and destroyed trust.
Maybe fear has made you silent when you should have spoken.
Maybe ambition has made you compromise when you should have obeyed.
Maybe you are exhausted from protecting an image of yourself that no longer matches what is happening inside.
You do not have to continue pretending before God.
Come to Jesus.
Not with a rehearsed defense.
Not with a carefully edited version of your past.
Not with the claim that everyone else was wrong and you were always innocent.
Come with the truth.
Confess what is yours to confess.
Repent of what is yours to repent of.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And begin walking in the newness of life He gives.
The promise of 1 John 1:9 remains precious:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
It is an invitation to come out of hiding.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes forgiveness possible through Christ and produces a changed life.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about exposing biblical scandals.
It is about seeing how Scripture confronts our hearts and leads us toward Jesus.
From pride to repentance.
From fear to faith.
From spiritual pretense to honest surrender.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the historical facts of our past.
Not by pretending that sin never happened.
But by redeeming sinners, forgiving guilt, transforming hearts, and giving His people a new future in Him.
And if this story has touched something you have been carrying privately, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not need to publish your deepest secrets for strangers to read.
But you can make a simple declaration of faith.
And if you have experienced the mercy of Jesus after a season of failure, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Your words might remind them that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Christ is still able to transform a life.
Do not keep this message to yourself if someone you love needs to hear it.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and those who are still searching for truth to follow along.
Because spiritual growth is not sustained by one emotional moment.
It is nurtured through continued attention to God's Word, prayer, fellowship, obedience, and dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
Not because God's love can be purchased.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life of love and obedience to Him.
But voluntary financial generosity can also be one meaningful expression of that love.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”

It helps create room for more Scripture-based articles, more discipleship resources, more encouragement, and more opportunities to reach people who may be spiritually exhausted, confused, or searching for hope.
Think of the person who is one message away from opening a Bible again.
The believer who has been silently struggling with guilt.
The young Christian who wants to grow but does not know where to begin.
The family member who has stopped attending church and needs to be reminded of the truth of the Gospel.
And there is something beautiful about giving not because you expect something from God in return, but because you are grateful for what Christ has already done.
These items can become useful reminders of Scripture, thoughtful gifts, and opportunities to begin conversations about faith.
It is the mission.
These resources are meant to encourage continued learning and spiritual nourishment, not replace the Bible, a faithful local church, or personal fellowship with other believers.
There is no need for guilt.
No need for pressure.
The Gospel itself is freely proclaimed because salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something anyone can buy.
And that brings us back to the frightened king.
Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner because he feared him.
His title could not give him courage.
His crown could not guarantee security.
His father's name could not preserve the dynasty.
And the commander on whom he depended was preparing to leave.
What a painful picture of the limitations of earthly power.
But what a powerful contrast to the hope we have in Jesus.
Earthly kingdoms rise and fall.
Reputations can collapse.
Influential people can walk away.
Even the strongest human arrangements can fail.
Yet Jesus Christ remains the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8).
He is not frightened by the instability of this world.
He is not threatened by the schemes of men.
He does not need manipulation to preserve His throne.
And He does not abandon those who truly belong to Him.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
What am I holding so tightly that I have forgotten how to trust Jesus?
Do not answer too quickly.
Let the question reach beneath your public image.
Beneath your achievements.
Beneath your anger.
Beneath the fear you rarely admit.
And when you recognize what has been ruling your heart, bring it before Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not losing an earthly crown.
It is spending your life protecting a throne in your heart that belongs to Jesus.
You may lose the throne you fought to keep, but in surrendering to Christ, you discover the King your soul was always meant to trust.
